A burrow is a hole or tunnel that an animal digs into the ground to live in. Think of it as an underground home — one that the animal makes itself, using its claws, snout, or body to push and scrape the earth away.

From the outside, a burrow usually looks like a small, round opening in the ground — an entrance hole. But inside, it goes much deeper. It can be a simple short tunnel, or it can be a complex underground network with multiple passages, turns, and rooms. Some burrows have separate spaces for sleeping, for raising babies, and even for storing food.

Many animals make burrows:

  • Rabbits are perhaps the most well-known burrowers. A network of connected rabbit burrows is called a warren.
  • Foxes, badgers, and groundhogs dig deep, sturdy burrows.
  • Moles create long tunnel systems just under the surface of the soil.
  • Prairie dogs build enormous underground towns with thousands of burrows linked together.
  • Some birds, like puffins and kingfishers, also dig burrows into soft earth or riverbanks to nest in.
  • Certain insects and reptiles (like some beetles and lizards) dig burrows too.

Animals make burrows for several reasons, and the same burrow often serves more than one purpose:

  • Safety from predators — underground and hidden, they are hard to reach.
  • Shelter from harsh weather — burrows stay cool in summer and surprisingly warm in winter.
  • A safe place to raise young — babies are protected from the outside world.
  • Hibernation — some animals sleep through winter inside their burrow.
  • Food storage — some animals store food in side chambers of the burrow.

This is important for precision:

  • A hole is just any opening — it has no meaning about who made it or why. A burrow is always made by an animal, on purpose, as a home.
  • A tunnel is just a passageway. A burrow is a home — it has an entrance, depth, and is meant to be lived in.
  • A nest is usually built above the ground from twigs, leaves, or grass. A burrow is dug into the ground.
  • A den can be a natural space (like a cave or a hollow log) that an animal simply moves into. A burrow, strictly speaking, is dug by the animal itself. However, in everyday speech, people sometimes use "den" and "burrow" interchangeably, especially for foxes and bears.
  • A lair is a more dramatic word, often used for dangerous or predatory animals, and it doesn't specify whether it was dug or found. "Lair" feels sinister; "burrow" feels cozy and small.

"Burrow" as a noun carries a sense of smallness, coziness, and hiddenness. It feels intimate — a snug, private space just big enough for the animal that made it. When you picture a burrow, you think of a creature curled up safely underground, sheltered from the world above.

• The rabbit darted into its burrow just as the fox approached.
  • The badger had dug a burrow so deep that no dog could reach it.
  • Scientists found an ancient prairie dog burrow system stretching beneath an entire field.
  • The fox's burrow had three entrances and a wide sleeping chamber at the end.

A burrow is specifically something dug into the earth. If an animal simply hides under a rock or in a hollow tree, that space is not a burrow — because the animal didn't dig it. The act of digging is built into the very idea of a burrow.
